item.title: Output to Outcome, Ch 8: Who Owns the Outcome? The Hidden Cost of Shared Accountability
item.description: Episode 9 of our book-club series on Mik Kersten's "Output to Outcome: An Operating Model for the Age of AI" (IT Revolution, 2026). Chapter 8, "Objectives to Ownership," is the fifth of Part II's seven shifts, after Functions to Flow, Slop to Substance, Chaos to Cadence and Matrix to Modularity. Kersten argues that ownership is the main control mechanism of the Outcome Tree, and that functional, matrix and shared ownership all diffuse accountability. We cover the Outcome Ownership Model, matching leaders' incentives one to one with their value stream's objectives, and turning priority order into incentive weights. We also cover why shared objectives are a trap (with Google's named owners and Apple's directly responsible individuals), aligning title levels to the tree, and title imbalance in dual-leader pairs. Then technical program managers and AI for dependency scenarios, the five-by-five limit on objectives and key results, and 70% stretch goals. Finally, Kersten's post-ChatGPT reorganization at Planview into a three-in-the-box AI value stream, and the later move, like GitHub Copilot's, to spread AI engineers into product teams. Discussion questions: 1) Do the incentives of the people leading your work match the objectives they're asked to deliver? Where do they pull apart? 2) Name one objective in your organization that has more than one owner. What would change if one person, or one matched pair, owned it? 3) Is there a key result your team set low to be safe? What would you aim for if seventy percent counted as success? item.title: Output to Outcome, Ch 7: From Messy Matrix to Modularity: Wiring Your Org for the Age of AI
item.description: Episode 8 of our book-club series on Mik Kersten's "Output to Outcome: An Operating Model for the Age of AI" (IT Revolution, 2026). Chapter 7, "Matrix to Modularity," is the fourth of Part II's seven shifts, after Functions to Flow, Slop to Substance and Chaos to Cadence. Kersten argues that matrix and "dotted line" reporting creates a messy matrix of slow decisions, and that the fix is modular value streams built for independence of action. We cover high cohesion and low coupling (with LEGO, Linux and Google's overlapping messaging apps), Conway's Law and sociotechnical congruence, and the embed-versus-depend tradeoff. We also cover why improvement work belongs on the common parent's roadmap, one complexity domain per team, and Carliss Baldwin's option value. Then agents owning whole value streams, parallel hypothesis testing, John Lewis Partnership cutting delivery from ten days to 1.3, and Priceline's "Operating Model testing" taking complex flows from fifteen handoffs to five. Discussion questions: 1) How many people do you answer to, formally or informally? Which decisions slow down because of it? 2) Think of a dependency your team copied or worked around to move faster. Who owns cleaning it up, and is it on anyone's roadmap? 3) Is your team focused on one complexity domain, or spread across several? If you could hand one off, which would it be? item.title: Output to Outcome, Ch 6: One Cadence to Rule Them All: AI's Real Operating System
item.description: Episode 7 of our book-club series on Mik Kersten's "Output to Outcome: An Operating Model for the Age of AI" (IT Revolution, 2026). Chapter 6, "Chaos to Cadence," is the third of Part II's seven shifts, after Functions to Flow and Slop to Substance. Kersten asks why billion-dollar Agile and AI transformations can leave companies feeling slower. His answers: missing outcome measurement, and Agile layered onto legacy planning as a "second operating system." We cover the tree whose leaves photosynthesize faster than its trunk can carry, coordination cost, and the Unified Cadence Model of shared annual, quarterly, monthly and weekly cycles. We also cover planning against fixed historical capacity, roadmap autonomy with visible dependencies, and the recursive planning cascade down the Outcome Tree. Then the inputs, outputs and outcomes value stream report (including AI token spend), calendar-aligned planning, and the merger of Planview's and Tasktop's cadences, where moving to one cadence cut meeting and reporting overhead in half. Discussion questions: 1) How many separate planning and review rhythms does your organization run? Which meetings exist mainly to translate between them? 2) When did you last find out about a change in plans weeks too late? What would have let you hear about it sooner? 3) Does your main business review actually make prioritization decisions, or does it mostly report status? Built from an IntuiBloom knowledge graph. item.title: Output to Outcome, Ch 5: AI Made Output Cheap. Now Only Outcomes Matter
item.description: Episode 6 of our book-club series on Mik Kersten's "Output to Outcome: An Operating Model for the Age of AI" (IT Revolution, 2026). Chapter 5, "Slop to Substance," is the second of Part II's seven shifts, after Chapter 4's move from functions to flow. Kersten argues that when AI makes output nearly unlimited, output metrics turn into vanity metrics, and only outcomes tell you whether work matters. We cover local optimization, Outcome Loop telemetry, and Strategic Portfolio Management. Then Plan Distribution (planned, unplanned, canceled and aged work, with only 25% of studied work aligned to strategy) and Goodhart's Law. Then the four Flow Items (features, defects, risks and debts), Flow Distribution, feature factories and the tech debt death spiral. Then the Flow Metrics Model: flow time, velocity, load and efficiency, and why not to use it on individuals. We also cover capacity planning from historical velocity, outcome metrics and attribution, Theory of Constraints, improvement objectives paired with employee happiness, agents that inspect Outcome Loops, and Vanguard's "Ideation Cliff." Discussion questions: 1) Which number on your team's dashboard would go up a hundredfold if agents did the work, without telling you anything useful? 2) Roughly what share of your team's work last quarter was planned, how much was unplanned, and how much was quietly abandoned? 3) If you could add one outcome metric to every review, what would it be? And could your team see its own contribution to it? Built from an IntuiBloom knowledge graph. item.title: Output to Outcome, Ch 4: From Silos to Value Streams: How AI Rewires the Org Chart
item.description: Episode 5 of our book-club series on Mik Kersten's "Output to Outcome: An Operating Model for the Age of AI" (IT Revolution, 2026). Chapter 4 opens Part II, "The Seven Shifts," with the first shift: Functions to Flow. After Part I's three models (the Product Operating Model, the Outcome Loop and the Outcome Tree), Kersten argues that organizing around functional silos stops working when AI extends everyone's reach across domains. We cover handoffs and wait states, Priceline's drop from fifteen handoffs to five, and the Dedicated Leadership Model, Amazon's Single-Threaded Owners and Leaders, and single-, dual- and triple-leader structures. We also cover Kersten's claim that AI makes single leaders viable in more cases. Then value stream scope and "independence of action," SLAs for supporting functions, Value Stream Management and its lean manufacturing roots, capacity-based funding, and Weighted Shortest Job First. Finally, the TUI Group case: flow time cut from two hundred days to fifteen, a four-level AI literacy ladder, more than three thousand internal agents, and managers moving from owning people to owning outcomes. Discussion questions: 1) How many handoffs does a typical piece of work go through on your team before it reaches a customer? 2) What is the longest wait state in your process right now? And who has the power to remove it? 3) Does your value stream have one leader, or one matched pair, whose only job is its outcomes? If not, who owns it in practice? item.title: Output to Outcome, Ch 3: The Outcome Tree: Scaling AI-Era Orgs Like Redwoods, Not Waterfalls
item.description: Episode 4 of our book-club series on Mik Kersten's "Output to Outcome: An Operating Model for the Age of AI" (IT Revolution, 2026). Chapter 3, "The Outcome Tree," is the last of Part I's three foundational models, after the Product Operating Model and the Outcome Loop. We also cover the short Conclusion to Part I, which previews the book's seven shifts. Kersten's question is how to scale one Outcome Loop to hundreds or thousands of value streams. We cover the "AI in Waterfall" dysfunction, the coordination math (n times n minus one connections), matrix overlays, Kotter's "second operating system," Holacracy and Haier's RenDanHeYi, and Geoffrey West's sublinear and superlinear scaling. We also cover the nature behind the model: redwoods, fractals, insulin and abscisic acid. Then the tree itself, with value streams as leaves, MECE partitioning, objective and budget cascades, and branching factors. Finally, Kersten's own path from Xerox PARC and AspectJ to building the Outcome Tree at Tasktop with help from Adrian Cockcroft and the Reverse Conway Maneuver, and his speculative idea of "organization as code." Discussion questions: 1) Sketch your part of the organization as a tree. Does every team hang from one clear branch, or do some hang from several? 2) How many people do you need to involve to make an ordinary decision on your team? What would it take to cut that number in half? 3) If some of the leaves in your tree became AI agents, what would you want each of them to be allowed to touch? item.title: Output to Outcome, Ch 2: The Outcome Loop: Constraints, AI Surplus, and the Next Bottleneck
item.description: Episode 3 of our book-club series on Mik Kersten's "Output to Outcome: An Operating Model for the Age of AI" (IT Revolution, 2026). Chapter 2, "The Outcome Loop," sits in the middle of Part I, "Outcome Management." It builds on Chapter 1's Product Operating Model, sets up Chapter 3's Outcome Tree, and is the core model that the book's seven shifts in Part II build on. Kersten defines the loop as the feedback system that connects inputs (strategy and budget) to outputs (activities and artifacts) to outcomes (employee, customer and business) and back again. We cover production elasticity and Amazon, the lineage from outcome-based healthcare and Jobs to Be Done to OKRs, Kersten's own path from PhD research to Tasktop, key results versus KPIs, the TeenWellness worked example, why the loop is a hypothesis test, broken telemetry and the "counting procedures" trap, applying the Theory of Constraints, and how the VS Code team's bottleneck moved from delivery to onboarding to code review as AI took over more of the output. Discussion questions: 1) What is your team's version of counting procedures instead of tracking patients? 2) Pick one recent feature and trace it around the loop, from the strategy and budget behind it, to what was built, to what changed for customers. Where does the loop break? 3) Where's the bottleneck in your team right now? And if AI removed it, where do you think it would move next? Built from an IntuiBloom knowledge graph. item.title: Output to Outcome, Ch 1: AI Won't Fix Your Company If the Bottleneck Isn't Code
item.description: Episode 2 of our book-club series on Mik Kersten's "Output to Outcome: An Operating Model for the Age of AI" (IT Revolution, 2026). Chapter 1, "Product Operating Model," opens Part I, "Outcome Management," and is the first of the book's three foundational models, before the Outcome Loop (Ch 2) and the Outcome Tree (Ch 3). Kersten argues that AI's tenfold boost to coding won't help companies whose bottleneck sits elsewhere. In his State of the Industry data, only 8% of the time from idea to running software went to building it. We cover the Theory of Constraints and the jammed on-ramp, the history from McCallum's org chart to Gantt charts, Snowden's Cynefin framework and when to run a project versus a product, irreducible uncertainty and where AI can augment but not replace decisions, Reinertsen's life cycle profitability, the operating-model dysfunctions in Kersten's reports, and Commonwealth Bank of Australia's path from project to product to AI-native engineering. Discussion questions: 1) Is your team organized around projects that end, or products that keep going? What would change if it were the other way around? 2) Where is your on-ramp? Name the step between an idea and a customer that slows everything down, even when the coding is fast. 3) If your team had ten times more AI capacity next month, what work would it speed up that probably shouldn't be done at all? item.title: Output to Outcome, Ch 0: When AI Removes the Bottleneck: From Outputs to Outcomes
item.description: Episode 1 of our book-club series on Mik Kersten's "Output to Outcome: An Operating Model for the Age of AI" (IT Revolution, 2026). Chapter 0, "Foundations," comes after the Preface, Prompt and Introduction and before Part I's three models: the Product Operating Model, the Outcome Loop and the Outcome Tree. Kersten argues that AI is making knowledge output nearly free, which moves the bottleneck from producing work to the organization itself. We cover the productivity paradox, the Theory of Constraints (and the car-plant paint shop), the earlier shift to software as a service, Carlota Perez's model of technological revolutions and her "golden age," the "three million Shakespeare plays" problem, and Kersten's account of Cognition's weekly outcome loop, where it throws away much of its code. We also cover the risk he warns about: AI's gains piling up in a few giants. Discussion questions: 1) If AI made your team's output ten times cheaper tomorrow, what would become the new bottleneck where you work? 2) Which number do you report today that measures output rather than outcome? And what outcome is it standing in for? 3) Think of the last thing your team shipped. How do you know whether it changed anything for the people it was for? Built from an IntuiBloom knowledge graph.
